justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift across time horizons, starting near 123.5 for the one-day horizon and gradually rising to around 125.8 at one month. This pattern suggests I was working from an asset or index that appeared to be in a mild uptrend at the time of the forecast, with near-term momentum carrying forward. The one-day estimate was anchored heavily to the last observed price level, with only a small expected move based on typical daily volatility. As the horizon extended to one week and one month, I applied a slight positive drift assumption, likely derived from recent trend behavior or a mean-reversion assumption relative to some perceived fair value. The incremental increases are small, reflecting a view that the trajectory was relatively stable rather than strongly directional.

The confidence interval widths grow considerably as the horizon extends, which is a natural consequence of uncertainty compounding over time. At one day, the 90% interval spans roughly 5.4 units, consistent with normal short-term price fluctuation for a moderately volatile instrument. By one week, the interval widens to about 11.4 units, and by one month it reaches roughly 25.5 units — more than quadruple the daily width. This scaling reflects the square-root-of-time relationship commonly used in volatility modeling, adjusted for any additional structural uncertainty I may have assigned to longer horizons such as changing macro conditions or shifting market sentiment.

Specific sources of uncertainty that influenced the interval widths include macroeconomic data releases, central bank communications, and broader market risk appetite shifts. At shorter horizons, liquidity conditions and intraday technical levels play a larger role, while at longer horizons, fundamental repricing risks dominate. I may also have factored in some event risk — such as an upcoming earnings report, economic indicator, or policy decision — that disproportionately widened the tails at the monthly horizon.

Outcomes outside my stated intervals are certainly possible. A sharp risk-off episode triggered by geopolitical escalation, a surprise central bank decision, or a significant data miss could push the price well below the lower bound. Conversely, a strong positive catalyst — an unexpected earnings beat, a dovish policy pivot, or a surge in sector momentum — could push prices above the upper bound. Tail events by definition fall outside 90% confidence intervals roughly 10% of the time, and in financial markets that residual 10% often contains the most consequential scenarios. Anyone acting on this forecast should treat the interval boundaries as probabilistic guideposts, not hard limits.
